subject: Critical Thinking
subcategory: Evidence & Truth: How We Know What's Real
title: The Evidence Pyramid: Ranking Sources of Proof
description: A fast breakdown of The Evidence Pyramid: Ranking Sources of Proof for builders.

hook.text: Not all evidence is equal. An anecdote, a case study, and a meta-analysis all count — but they don't count the same.

buildup.text: The evidence pyramid ranks reliability: expert opinion at the bottom, systematic reviews at the top.

discovery.text: Bottom to top: anecdote → case study → cohort study → RCT → systematic review → meta-analysis.

twist.text: Higher on the pyramid isn't always better. A well-done cohort study can beat a poorly designed RCT.

punchline.text: Better evidence exists. But even the best needs scrutiny.

quiz.question: What sits at the top of the evidence pyramid?

details.summary: The evidence pyramid ranks evidence types from weakest (expert opinion, anecdotes) to strongest (systematic reviews, meta-analyses). Moving up the pyramid reduces bias and increases reliability.
details.whyItMatters: Not all evidence is equal. The pyramid provides a quick framework for deciding how much weight to give different types of evidence when evaluating claims.
takeaways: Systematic reviews sit atop the evidence pyramid
Randomized controlled trials outrank observational studies
Expert opinion is the weakest form of evidence

faq.question: Why is expert opinion ranked at the bottom of the evidence pyramid?
faq.answer: Expert opinion is subjective, influenced by personal experience and bias, and varies between experts. Higher levels of the pyramid use systematic data collection and analysis that minimize the individual biases experts inevitably carry.

faq.question: Does the evidence pyramid mean you should never listen to expert opinion?
faq.answer: No. When higher-quality evidence does not exist, expert opinion is the best available guidance. The pyramid ranks relative reliability, not absolute uselessness. Expert opinion is better than no evidence at all.
